ABOUT fifteen minutes later, the great bell of the house rang for supper, and, as Leo did not come in, his aunt, Mrs. Pevensham, sent the parlour-maid to fetch him from the gardens. After a short while she came back and said that she could not find Master Leo at all. As he was often wont to wander down to the shore to watch the fishing boats come in, Mrs. Pevensham was not overly concerned at first, but when seven o’clock chimed, and Leo had not appeared, she grew quite distressed, and sent the two gardeners out to search for him, while she herself and his uncle searched the house from attic to cellar. At half-past seven the gardeners returned and reported that they could find no sign of the boy anywhere upon the grounds. They were all by now in a considerable state of alarm, and did not know what to do, when Mrs. Pevensham suddenly recalled that, only the day before, a foreign schooner had put into the harbour for repairs. She accordingly set off at once for the little port, accompanied by her husband and the head gardener. Young Elara, the harbourmaster’s daughter, who was quite beside herself with worry, pleaded to be allowed to come, but Mrs. Pevensham refused, as she feared there might be some unpleasantness with the sailors. On arriving at the quay, however, she found the schooner had already departed, and it was clear their leaving had been hasty, for a coil of new rope and a half-mended sail lay abandoned on the pier. Having sent the gardener to rouse the coastguard, she hurried home, and despatched messages to all the constables in the neighbouring villages, telling them to be on the watch for a young boy who may have been carried off by foreign sailors. She then ordered the carriage to be brought round, and, after begging her husband and the frightened servants to take some supper, she drove off towards Blackwood Creek with a groom. She had not, however, gone more than a mile when she heard the sound of someone running behind her, and, looking back, saw young Elara dashing up the road, her face streaked with tears and her hair undone. ‘Oh, I am so sorry, Mrs. Pevensham,’ the girl panted, ‘but I cannot rest while Leo is missing. Please, do not be cross with me; if you had seen how he looked at the sea, you would know he did not run away. You will not make me go back, will you? I cannot! I will not!’ The lady could not help but be moved by the fierce loyalty in the young girl’s face, and her devotion to Leo was plain to see, so leaning out of the carriage, she patted her arm gently, and said, ‘Well, Elara, if you will not go back I suppose you must come with us, but you must have my shawl at least.’ ‘Oh, never mind a shawl! I want Leo!’ cried the girl, clambering in, and they drove on to the coastguard’s station. There Mrs. Pevensham enquired of the officer if any boy answering Leo’s description had been reported, but he had no news for her. The officer, however, sent signals up and down the coast, and assured her that every boat would be hailed and searched, and, after forcing a cup of hot tea upon Elara, Mrs. Pevensham drove on to Whitecliff, a fishing hamlet some three miles distant, which she knew was a place where smugglers sometimes landed their wares. Here they woke the local constable, but could get no useful word from him, and, after searching the entire length of the beach, they turned the horses’ heads for home, and arrived back at the manor near midnight, utterly exhausted and with spirits sunk low. They found Mr. Pevensham and the gardeners waiting at the gate-house with lamps, as the long drive was shrouded in darkness. Not a single clue to Leo’s whereabouts had been found. The schooner had been intercepted off the point, but he was not on board, and the captain had explained their sudden departure by saying the winds had turned favourable, and they had cast off in a hurry to catch the tide. Indeed, the crew seemed genuinely concerned to hear of Leo’s disappearance, as he had spent the previous afternoon talking to them, and two of the sailors had volunteered to stay behind and aid in the search. The seaward caves had been checked, and the whole of the cliff path thoroughly explored, but to no avail. It was quite plain that, for this night at least, Leo was truly gone; and it was in a state of profoundest misery that Mrs. Pevensham and the girl walked up to the house, the groom following with the tired horses. It was a grim and silent meal, as no one had the heart to speak, and even the normally cheerful cook was pale and subdued, as she was very fond of the boy.

‘That was very remarkable,’ said Mr. Pevensham, rubbing his eyes. ‘I have never known a storm to come and go so quickly. It must have been an electrical phenomenon of some sort.’

‘Leo!’ screamed Mrs. Pevensham, and she flew out of the room, with Elara and Mr. Pevensham close behind her.

And there, at the top of the great oak staircase, stood Leo. He was very pale, and in his dark hair there were little phosphorescent stars of sea-foam that glimmered and faded. His eyes had a strange and beautiful light in them, like the reflection of the moon on deep water. In one hand he held a spray of what looked like delicate white coral, from which hung tiny, bell-shaped flowers that were not of this earth, and in the other he carried a small, intricately carved box, inlaid with mother-of-pearl.

In a moment they were all crowding around him. Mrs. Pevensham covered him with kisses, and Elara clung to his hand, while Mr. Pevensham patted him on the back with a vehemence that was quite unlike his usual composure. The gardeners, who had been lingering in the hall, let out a cheer, and the maids came running up from the kitchen, laughing and crying all at once.

‘My dearest boy! Where have you been?’ cried his mother. ‘We have been half-mad with worry! We thought you had been carried off by smugglers, or drowned in the sea!’

‘I am very sorry if I have frightened you,’ said Leo, in a voice that was soft and clear as a distant bell, ‘but I have been far away. I have been with the Old Mariner, and I have brought him peace.’

He smiled a strange, sad smile, and held out the little box. ‘The prophecy is fulfilled,’ he said to Elara, who was gazing up at him with wide, adoring eyes. ‘He was the sinner, for he had hoarded his grief and chained his soul to this world. Mr. Pevensham took the little box and opened it. Inside, lying on a bed of dark green seaweed, was a collection of the most wonderful jewels he had ever seen. There were ropes of pearls like frozen moonlight, and sapphires the colour of the deep ocean, and emeralds that shimmered like shallow water over sand. There were also strange, unearthly gems that seemed to have captured the light of forgotten stars, and golden coins from shipwrecks a thousand years old.

‘My dear boy,’ exclaimed Mr. Pevensham, ‘do you have any idea of the value of these things? They must be worth a fortune! I am very much of the opinion that the Mariner, whoever he was, has behaved in a most handsome and gentlemanly manner. However, now that you have them, you must be extremely careful, for I am afraid that the tax assessors will be most interested, and your mother’s family will be quite insufferable.’

‘But where is he?’ whispered Mrs. Pevensham, looking around the hall as if she expected to see the spectre of the Old Mariner appear.

‘He is at rest,’ said Leo, ‘and he will trouble this house no more. But he wished me to give you this.’ He stepped forward and handed the strange, flowering coral to his mother. As she took it, the blossoms chimed with a faint, ethereal music, and then turned to glittering dust in her hand. ‘He says you have the kindest heart he has ever known.’

Then Leo turned to Elara. ‘And he has not forgotten you, who were so brave.’ From the box he took a single, perfect black pearl, strung on a fine silver chain. ‘He said you stood by me, when even the waves tried to turn me back.’ He fastened the chain around her neck, and his cold fingers sent a little shiver through her, but she did not falter, and her eyes shone with happiness.

‘Come,’ said Leo, taking his father’s hand, ‘I must show you where he lay.’

They all followed him, the servants creeping behind with lighted candles, as he led them down the grand staircase and through a series of long, echoing corridors. He did not seem to hesitate for a moment, but walked with a sure and steady step, as if he had trodden this path a hundred times before. He led them down into the cold, damp wine-cellars, past barrels of ancient port and dusty bottles of claret, until they reached a solid brick wall at the very back.

‘It was here,’ Leo said quietly, and he pressed his hand against a particular brick. There was a low grinding sound, and a section of the wall swung slowly inwards, revealing a dark and narrow passage from which came the salty smell of the sea and the sound of distant waves.

Mr. Pevensham recoiled for a moment. ‘Good heavens, Leo! A secret passage! I had no idea. This is most improper; it is a direct invitation to smugglers and other undesirable persons. I shall have it bricked up first thing in the morning.’

‘Not until we have seen,’ said Leo, and he stepped into the darkness.

The passage was long and winding, and sloped steeply downwards. The air grew colder, and the sound of the sea grew louder, until at last they emerged into a large, domed sea-cave. The moonlight streamed in through a high fissure in the rock, illuminating the cavern with a ghostly silver light and turning the pools of water on the floor into plates of polished metal. The walls were slick with moisture and covered in shimmering green algae. It was a place of wild and solemn beauty.

In a corner, half buried in the sand and tangled in the rotting remains of a fishing net, lay a human skeleton. A rusted chain was wound about its wrists, and its bony fingers were curled as if in supplication. As they all stared in silent awe, a little wave lapped into the cave and washed over the bones, and a spray of luminous sea-moss that had been clinging to the skull detached itself and floated away, glowing for a moment in the darkness before it was gone.

‘We must give him a Christian burial,’ said Mrs. Pevensham, her voice trembling. ‘It is the least we can do.’

‘He shall be buried in the corner of the churchyard,’ said Mr. Pevensham, ‘the corner that looks out over the sea. I shall speak to the vicar myself.’

They stood there for a few more moments in silence, and then, as Leo took his mother’s hand, they turned and made their way back up the dark passage to the house.

A week later, a small funeral was held. The old skeleton, which the local doctor had declared to be at least two hundred years old, was placed in a simple coffin and interred in the quietest corner of the St. Giles churchyard. Leo and Elara laid a wreath of wildflowers on the fresh earth. It was a beautiful autumn day, and the sun shone brightly on the grey stones and the distant, sparkling sea.

That evening, as they sat in the drawing-room after dinner, Leo walked over to where Elara was sitting by the fire, reading a book of fairy tales. He was holding the pearl and jewel box.

‘My father says that these belong to me now,’ he said, ‘and that I may do with them as I wish.’

‘They are very beautiful,’ said Elara, looking up from her book.

‘I should like you to have them,’ Leo said simply. ‘You were going to help me, after all. And love, he said, is stronger than the sea.’

Elara’s cheeks grew very pink. ‘Oh, I couldn’t possibly!’ she stammered. ‘Your father said they were worth a fortune.’

‘Then we shall have a fortune together,’ said Leo, and before she could protest, he knelt down beside her and kissed her.

Mr. Pevensham, who had been observing this scene from behind his newspaper, coughed loudly. ‘I must say, Leo,’ he remarked, ‘that while I admire your generosity, I cannot help but feel that offering a young lady what amounts to a significant portion of the Crown Jewels as a preliminary to a proposal is perhaps a trifle precipitate. I fear it sets a dangerous precedent. However,’ he added, putting down his paper and smiling at the two of them, ‘I am bound to admit that it is a very fine pearl.’

And from that day on, the Pevensham Manor was at peace, and the only spirit that haunted its halls was the gentle echo of the sea. The old butler maintained that on stormy nights you could still hear the faint sound of a lute, but no one really believed him, and even the maids were no longer afraid to walk the corridors after dark. Leo and Elara were, of course, married as soon as they were old enough, and were as happy as they deserved to be; and as for the Mariner’s treasure, it was locked away in a bank vault in London, though Mr. Pevensham was sometimes heard to mutter that it was a great pity he could not wear the sapphires himself, as they would have gone so wonderfully well with his new evening coat.

Cecil, for his part, was so entirely devoted to his wife that he was considered by many of his bachelor friends to be quite lost to civilized society, a sentiment he would have heartily endorsed.

It was on a fine June afternoon, when the family was once more gathered at the Chase, that the first discordant note in this domestic symphony was sounded. A letter arrived, addressed to the Duke of Cheshire, bearing the seal of a firm of London solicitors, Messrs. Grumbles, Grumbles, and Gripe. Mr. Otis, who had a profound distrust of English lawyers, which he ranked only slightly below his distrust of English plumbing, watched with a frown as Cecil broke the seal.

The little Duke read the letter, his brow furrowing in confusion. He read it a second time, and a flush of indignation crept up his neck. ‘Well, I’m dashed,’ he exclaimed, a phrase he had picked up from his American brothers-in-law and which he employed on occasions of extreme vexation.

‘What is it, Cecil?’ asked Virginia, placing a hand on his arm.

‘It is a letter of the most impertinent and preposterous nature,’ he said, handing it to Mr. Otis. ‘It seems we have an uninvited relation.’

The Minister adjusted his spectacles and read the document aloud, his voice taking on a dry, forensic tone. ‘Yes, sir. Many times.’

‘And he gave you this box of jewels?’

‘He did.’

I went with him to the Garden of Death and I pleaded for him with the Angel of Death. And the Angel had mercy.’

She paused, and the silence in the chamber was absolute. Even Mr. Gripe seemed, for a moment, at a loss for words.

‘Those jewels,’ Virginia continued, her voice soft but unwavering, ‘were not payment. They were proof. Proof that his soul was free. He gave them to me so that I would remember him, and remember that forgiveness is possible, even after centuries of sin. To take them away would be to say that his suffering meant nothing. It would be to steal the last hope from a soul at peace. They are not mere diamonds and rubies, my lords. They are the tears of a forgiven ghost.’

She finished, and stood there, a strange light in her eyes. One of the old lords, the Earl of Ruston, a man famous for his gruff demeanour, was seen to be openly wiping his eyes with a large silk handkerchief. Another blew his nose with a sound like a trumpet. A wave of pure, unadulterated sentiment, a thing most alien to that august chamber, swept through the room.

Cecil took the heavy casket, which Mr. Otis had insisted on bringing from the bank vault, and opened it. The jewels glittered in the moonlight with a fire that seemed almost alive.

‘He would be happy,’ Virginia whispered, touching the ruby necklace.

‘He is at peace, my love,’ said Cecil. ‘And so are we.’ He took her in his arms. ‘It is a curious thing, though. We seem to be the only family in England whose inheritance depends upon the testimony of a ghost.’

Mr. Otis, who had come out to join them, overheard the last remark. ‘Indeed,’ he said, looking at the contented couple and then out at the dark, silent park. ‘It only goes to show that in this country, it is not enough to have the law on your side. The house was no longer haunted by grief, but tenanted by a gentle sorrow.

‘It’s a funny thing, Cecil,’ he said, gesturing with his cigar at the ancient, moonlit edifice of the Chase. ‘When I bought this place, I thought I was buying a piece of real estate. And one Duke.’ He clapped Cecil fondly on the shoulder. ‘On the whole, I’d say I got a fair price. Fenwick was a man of immense and solemn dignity, who had served the Canterville estate for forty years and had viewed the arrival of the Americans with the same stoic resignation with which he might have greeted a swarm of locusts; he had seen ghosts, he had seen republicans, and he considered the latter to be the more disruptive phenomenon.

‘For me, Fenwick?’ asked Virginia, as the butler presented it to her.

‘It is addressed to the house, your Grace. The station-master at Ascot thought it best to direct it to you, as you are known to be the… the primary correspondent in the family.’ This was Fenwick’s delicate way of saying that Virginia was the only one who did not view modern inventions like the telegraph as a form of vulgar witchcraft.

‘It appears, my dear, that the peace of Canterville is about to evolve once more.’

‘Good heavens,’ said the Duke, pausing with his toast halfway to his mouth. ‘What is it? Not another war in the Crimea? Has Parliament finally decided to abolish the House of Lords?’

‘Something far more significant, Cecil. My family is coming to visit. They will be here this afternoon.’

‘Yes,’ said Virginia, rereading the telegram with evident pleasure. ‘Papa, Mamma, Washington, and the twins. Virginia, my love, your father has a more highly developed sense of irony than I have ever given him credit for.’ He sighed, a long, theatrical sigh of the truly put-upon aristocrat. ‘Very well. Then came Washington, now a rather serious young man with a burgeoning political career in New York, who carried a briefcase full of what he called ‘important documents’ and looked upon the crumbling grandeur of the Chase with the pained expression of a sanitary inspector.

Last, and most certainly not least, came the twins. Franklin and Harrison, known to their family and a terrified legion of Oxford dons simply as Frank and Harry, were no longer the small, catapult-wielding terrors of old. They had grown into two startlingly handsome young men, dressed in the height of fashion, whose angelic faces and charming smiles concealed souls dedicated to the holy cause of causing trouble. They vaulted from the carriage before it had even come to a full stop and immediately began to inspect their old haunts with the proprietary air of generals returning to a favourite battlefield.

Virginia, who had come out to greet them, hugged them all with genuine delight, while the Duke looked on with the weary but affectionate smile of a man who has married not just a woman, but a force of nature.

It lacks the classical simplicity of a well-placed frog, perhaps, but the ambition is to be commended.’

The moon was high and full, bathing the park in a wash of silver, and from somewhere in the distance, a nightingale, a bird with a keen sense of theatrical timing, began to sing.

‘They are not so bad, are they?’ Virginia said, leaning her head against his shoulder.

‘My love,’ he replied, ‘they are magnificent. They are a force of nature. They are utterly and completely impossible, and I find, to my great astonishment, that I am rather fond of them. Your father has offered to buy the fishing rights to the carp-pond and turn it into a public resort. He says it has “untapped potential.”’

‘And what did you say?’

‘I told him I would consider it, if he would agree to be the first to test the diving board. For centuries, this house was famous for its silence. Its ghost. Its sorrow. Now…’

He gestured out at the great, dark mass of the Chase, where light still burned in half a dozen windows. It was no longer a place of echoing halls and faded memories. It was alive. It was loud. Virginia smiled. ‘It looks like the twins are attempting to communicate with Mars.’

For the peace that had finally settled over the ancient house was not the sterile, silent peace of the grave that the poor ghost had so desperately craved. It was the messy, complicated, and gloriously alive peace of a family; a peace not of endings, but of endless, and endlessly surprising, new beginnings. And in the heart of that living peace, the old ghost of Canterville could, at last, truly rest.

Each stroke echoed through the silent house like a hammer-blow of fate, and with the twelfth and final clang, a peal of thunder, a truly prodigious and quite unseasonable clap, shook the very foundations of Canterville Chase. It was followed, not by rain, but by a rushing, tearing sound from the landing above, and then a great crash, as if some heavy piece of furniture had been overturned.

‘Good heavens, what is that?’ cried Mrs. Otis, springing to her feet and pressing a hand to her heart.

‘It is the gypsies returning for the silver!’ exclaimed Washington, seizing a heavy Georgian salt-cellar as a makeshift weapon.

‘Nonsense,’ said Mr. Otis firmly, though he himself had turned rather pale. ‘The gypsies are under lock and key. It is more likely a structural failure. I knew I should have had that north wing surveyed.’

Only the little Duke of Cheshire seemed to have a different idea. ‘Virginia!’ he cried, his face lighting up with a wild hope. ‘It came from the Tapestry Chamber!’

Without another word, he darted out of the room, the others following close behind him, a strange procession of terrified hope and practical concern. They streamed up the great oak staircase, their lanterns casting long, dancing shadows that seemed to mock their anxiety. They burst into the Tapestry Chamber to find it, at first glance, quite empty. The furniture was undisturbed, the moonlight streamed through the window onto the faded huntsmen, who seemed to mock them with their silent horns. There was no sign of the disturbance, no clue as to the great noise they had heard.

Mrs. Otis gave a low moan and was about to collapse into her husband’s arms when a faint movement caught her eye. By the great fireplace, where before there had been only solid wall, the panelling seemed to waver and shimmer, like air above a hot stove. As they watched, breathless, the wall itself appeared to dissolve, and through the spectral opening stepped Virginia.

She was very pale, and in her eyes was a distant, starlit look, as if she had just returned from a long journey to some unknown country. Her golden hair was slightly dishevelled, and her white dress was touched here and there with what looked like grave-dust, but her expression was one of perfect and profound serenity. In her hands she held a small, oblong casket, exquisitely wrought of old Italian silver and studded with lapis lazuli.

For a moment, nobody moved or spoke. They simply stared, as if she were an apparition herself. It was the little Duke who broke the spell. With a choked cry of ‘Virginia!’, he rushed forward and fell on his knees before her, seizing her free hand and covering it with kisses.

‘My darling, you are safe! I knew you would return! I never lost faith!’

‘Of course she is safe,’ said Mr. Otis, recovering his voice, which was now thick with emotion. He strode forward and put his arms around his daughter. ‘My dear child, where have you been? We have been out of our minds with worry. We had the police out, and the carp-pond dragged, and I have sent telegrams to every corner of the county.’

Mrs. Otis, weeping with sheer relief, began alternately hugging her daughter and feeling her forehead for a fever. ‘Oh, my sweet girl, you are so cold! And your dress! You must have a hot bath at once, with Dr. Dobell’s patent restorative elixir. And then a good strong dose of tincture of quinine.’

Even the twins, for once speechless, crept up and stood beside their sister, their eyes wide with awe, while Washington put the salt-cellar down rather sheepishly.

‘I am quite well, Papa,’ Virginia said, in a low, musical voice that seemed new to them. ‘And I am not cold. I have been with the Ghost.’

A collective gasp went through the room.

‘He is gone,’ Virginia continued, her voice filled with a gentle pity. ‘He is at peace. The prophecy has been fulfilled. I wept for him, and I prayed for him, and the Angel of Death was merciful.’

She looked down at the casket in her hands. ‘He asked me to lead him to the Garden of Death. And when he was at rest, I found this waiting for me.’

She opened the lid. Inside, resting on a bed of faded violet velvet, lay a collection of the most magnificent jewels they had ever seen. There was a necklace of rubies, like drops of frozen blood, bracelets of emeralds that shone with a green inner fire, and ropes of pearls that shimmered like the moon on water. At the very centre lay a great diamond, cut in the shape of a rose, that glittered with a thousand colours.

‘Jiminy!’ whispered one of the twins. ‘It’s a pirate’s treasure!’

Mr. Otis took the casket from his daughter, his expression a comical mixture of paternal pride and financial suspicion. He took out the diamond rose, held it up to the light, and examined it with the critical eye of a man well-versed in the valuation of commodities. ‘The workmanship is sixteenth-century Florentine, if I’m not mistaken,’ he murmured, ‘and as for the stones… well, if they are real, and I have a strong suspicion that they are, they are worth a king’s ransom. Or,’ he added thoughtfully, ‘the entire annual budget of a small but prosperous state.’

He looked sternly at his daughter. ‘Virginia, this is a matter of some gravity. Did this… this ghost… give them to you as a gift? There may be inheritance taxes to consider. We must declare them.’

‘Oh, Hiram, for heaven’s sake, can you not think of taxes at a time like this?’ cried Mrs. Otis. ‘The child has been consorting with spirits and you are worried about customs!’

‘My dear,’ replied the Minister calmly, ‘it is precisely because she has been consorting with spirits that a practical approach is necessary. Ghosts are not known for their grasp of terrestrial law. I must insist, however, that these jewels are not yours to keep, Virginia. They are, without a doubt, heirlooms of the Canterville family, and they must be returned to the present Lord Canterville at once.’

Virginia smiled, a faint, knowing smile that made her look older than her years. ‘The Ghost said they were for me,’ she said simply. ‘He said they were a poor recompense for what his family had done to him, and a gift to the little girl who had saved his soul. But he would want you to do what is right, Papa.’

‘Right,’ echoed Mr. Otis, looking somewhat relieved. ‘Exactly. First thing in the morning, I shall write to Lord Canterville.’

‘But where was he?’ demanded Washington, his journalistic instincts taking over. ‘Where did you go?’

‘Show us the secret door!’ chorused the twins, prodding at the wainscoting.

Virginia laid a finger on a small, carved rosette in the panelling beside the fireplace. There was a faint click, and a section of the wall swung silently inwards, revealing a narrow, stone-lined passage, black and forbidding. A gust of cold, musty air, smelling of damp earth and centuries of disuse, blew into the room.

‘He is in there,’ she said softly. ‘At the end. He wants to be buried in consecrated ground. His name was Sir Simon de Canterville. He confessed it all to me. His wife’s brothers starved him to death in that little room, because he had murdered her. He was a wicked man, but he was very sorry for it.’

Mr. Otis took a lantern from one of the servants who had gathered, wide-eyed, in the doorway. ‘Washington, you and I will go. Cecil, you stay here with Virginia and the ladies.’

‘I am going with you,’ said the little Duke, his jaw set. ‘Virginia has been braver than any of us. I shall not leave her story to be verified by others.’

Mr. Otis looked at the determined young man, then at his daughter’s serene face, and nodded. ‘Very well. But you boys,’ he said, turning to the twins, ‘are to stay put. This is not one of your games.’

The three of them, Mr. Otis, Washington, and the Duke, stepped into the darkness of the passage, their lantern cutting a small, trembling circle of light in the oppressive gloom. The passage was no more than thirty feet long, and it ended in a low, arched doorway closed by a massive, iron-studded door. It was not locked, but rusted almost solid on its hinges, and it took the combined strength of all three men to force it open with a great, groaning shriek of metal.

They found themselves in a tiny, windowless cell, not much larger than a cupboard. Chained to a great iron ring in the wall was a human skeleton, which lay stretched out on the stone floor, its long, bony fingers seeming to grasp at an old-fashioned water-jug and platter that were placed just out of its reach. The jug was green with mould, and the platter held nothing but a little pile of dust.

It was a grim and piteous sight. Washington felt a little sick, and even Mr. Otis was silent for a full minute. The little Duke, his romantic notions of adventure colliding with this sordid reality, took off his hat in a gesture of respect.

‘This is what became of him,’ Mr. Otis said at last, his voice low and solemn. ‘Murdered by his own in-laws. It is a terrible business. Virginia was right. We must give him a Christian burial.’

A few days later, a simple funeral was held in the small churchyard at the edge of the Canterville estate. The ancient coffin, bearing the restored nameplate of ‘Sir Simon de Canterville’, was followed to its final resting place by the entire Otis family, the Duke of Cheshire, and all the household staff. In the leafless branches of a yew tree, a little bird sang as if it would break its heart, and the winter sun broke through the clouds just as the coffin was lowered into the earth. It was, as Mrs. Otis later remarked, all beautifully and poetically arranged.

Standing at the back of the small crowd was a tall, stooping man with grey hair and a melancholy expression, who had arrived from London the previous day. It was the present Lord Canterville, Sir Simon’s distant descendant. After the service, Mr. Otis took him aside and formally offered him the casket of jewels.

Lord Canterville waved a dismissive hand. ‘My dear Mr. Otis, please, I cannot possibly accept them,’ he said in a weary voice. ‘My family and I owe your charming daughter a debt of gratitude we can never repay. For three hundred years, that wretched ancestor of mine has disgraced the family name and made the Chase uninhabitable. Miss Virginia has performed a great service, not only to him, but to us. The jewels are hers, by right of conquest, so to speak. Indeed, I insist they be part of her dowry when she marries my young cousin, Cheshire, as I trust she now will.’

Mr. Otis, who found this aristocratic blend of gratitude and matchmaking rather baffling, simply bowed and agreed.

That evening, as twilight fell, Virginia and Cecil walked in the churchyard. They stood for a moment before the new, simple headstone that marked Sir Simon’s grave. The raw earth was already covered with flowers from the greenhouse.

‘You have been very brave,’ said Cecil, taking her hand.

‘He taught me what Life is,’ she said softly, ‘and what Death signifies, and why Love is stronger than both.’

The little Duke did not quite understand what she meant, but he drew her closer and kissed her, and the barren almond tree that grew against the churchyard wall suddenly, and quite out of season, burst into a cloud of delicate pink blossoms.

Back at the Chase, the American Minister was writing a long and detailed letter to a colleague in the State Department about the complexities of English inheritance law, while Mrs. Otis supervised the packing of the jewels into a modern safe he had ordered from London. Washington was in the library, attempting to write a sensational account of the whole affair for the New York Herald, but finding that the reality was somehow too quiet and too strange for print.

And in their bedroom, the twins were poring over a crude map they had drawn of the house, marking with a red crayon the spot where the secret passage began. They had already discovered that the passage had a second, even more secret branch, leading directly to the main pantry. Their plans for the future were ambitious, and involved a great deal of stolen jam.

The house was not silent. It was filled with the sounds of life: with arguments about politics, with the clatter of new machinery, with the distant shrieks of the twins, and with the laughter of a young girl who had looked into the eyes of Death and was not afraid. Canterville Chase had found peace at last, but it was not the peace of the grave. It was the noisy, vibrant, and thoroughly wonderful peace of a home.

When they had gone back to the house, and the last of the servants had retired to bed, a profound quiet did indeed settle over Canterville Chase, but it was a quiet of an altogether different quality from that which Sir Simon had so long craved. It was the quiet of a house breathing, a house whose ancient timbers, long accustomed to the clanking of spectral chains and the hollow groans of remorse, were now adjusting to the gentle snores of Mr. Otis, the soft rustle of Mrs. Otis turning a page in her latest volume on American herbal remedies, and the muffled thuds from the twins’ room that suggested a pillow-fight of epic proportions. Life had taken hold of the old house with a firm and reassuring grip.

A few weeks passed in this agreeable fashion. The little Duke of Cheshire was a near-permanent fixture, his pony cropping the grass in the park as if it were its own, and his days spent in a state of beatific devotion to Virginia. He followed her from room to room with the loyal and uncomprehending adoration of a handsome spaniel, content to hold her skeins of wool, to listen to her read, or simply to gaze at her as she sat sketching by the library window. Mr. Otis had written again to the State Department, this time on the curious English habit of allowing fiancés to be constantly underfoot before a marriage was even formally announced, and had received a reply that was, for once, quite unhelpful.

The first tremor to disturb this domestic paradise came, as such tremors often do, in the form of a letter, delivered on a silver salver by the footman. It bore a crest of such intimidating complexity that Washington remarked it looked less like a coat of arms and more like a diagram of a railway collision. Mrs. Otis, upon seeing it, gave a little gasp and immediately reached for her bottle of Dr. Dobell’s Tincture.

‘It is from the Duchess of Bolton,’ said Mr. Otis, adjusting his spectacles and breaking the formidable seal. ‘Cecil’s mother.’

‘Oh, Hiram!’ cried his wife. ‘I had hoped we should not have to deal with her until the wedding. I hear she is a woman of very formidable opinions.’

‘Well, my dear,’ said Mr. Otis, scanning the page, ‘it appears she is not content to wait. She writes that she is coming down from London to make our acquaintance. She will be arriving the day after to-morrow.’

A pall fell over the breakfast table. Virginia, who had been describing the colour of a sunset to Cecil, fell silent. The little Duke had the good grace to look deeply apologetic. ‘I am awfully sorry,’ he stammered. ‘My mother can be a bit… well, she is very particular. She thinks anything west of Kensington is the savage frontier.’

‘It is perfectly natural that she should wish to meet her son’s future bride and her family,’ said Mr. Otis with a diplomacy that had served him well in many a difficult negotiation. ‘We shall welcome her with true American hospitality.’

‘I hope she is not allergic to the Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent,’ said Washington drily, alluding to his recent failed attempt to clean a stubborn wine stain from the dining room carpet. ‘The smell is still rather pervasive in the east wing.’

The twins, who had been unusually quiet, exchanged a look of pure, unholy glee. A Duchess. A formidable Duchess. The possibilities were so intoxicating that they quite forgot to put marmalade in the sugar-bowl, a prank they had been carefully planning all morning.

The next two days were a flurry of anxious preparation. Mrs. Otis drove the household staff into a state of nervous exhaustion, insisting that every piece of silver be polished to a blinding sheen and that fresh antimacassars, a recent and, in her view, highly civilised purchase from London, be placed on every chair. She held a long and serious consultation with the cook about the menu, crossing off every American dish in a panic and replacing them with vague but grand-sounding French names she had found in a magazine. Mr. Otis, for his part, retired to the library to read up on the history of the peerage, a subject he found vastly more complicated and far less logical than the American constitution.

The Duchess of Bolton arrived not in a carriage but in a large, black, and funereal motor-car that coughed and sputtered its way up the avenue as if in protest at the bucolic surroundings. She was a tall, thin woman with a face like a Roman eagle and a quantity of dark purple silk arranged about her person. She alighted from the vehicle with the air of an empress stepping onto a newly conquered, and deeply unsatisfactory, province. Her son, Cecil, rushed forward to greet her, but was stopped by a gloved hand.

‘Cecil, you are looking flushed,’ she announced, her voice a low, chilling monotone. ‘This country air does not agree with you. It is too… damp.’ She surveyed the ancient, sun-dappled façade of Canterville Chase, and a look of profound distaste settled on her features. Her gaze swept over the waiting Otis family, who had assembled on the steps, and came to rest on Mr. Otis.

‘You must be the Minister,’ she said, not as a question, but as a statement of regrettable fact.

‘Hiram P. Otis, at your service, your Grace,’ he replied with a cheerful bow. ‘And this is my wife, Lucretia. My eldest son, Washington, and our daughter, Virginia.’ He omitted the twins, who were lurking behind a large stone urn, their faces alight with criminal intent.

The Duchess inclined her head a fraction of an inch in Mrs. Otis’s direction. ‘I trust you are well,’ she said, in a tone that suggested she neither trusted it nor cared. Her eyes, small and hard as jet beads, then fixed upon Virginia. She examined the girl from head to toe, her expression unchanging, as if she were pricing a piece of livestock and finding it wanting. Virginia, who had faced down a three-hundred-year-old ghost, felt a blush rise to her cheeks. There was something in the Duchess’s stare far more terrifying than any spectral horror.

‘So you are the girl who has captured my son’s heart,’ the Duchess stated. She turned to Cecil. ‘She is very… golden. An American trait, I believe.’

Dinner that evening was a trial of monumental proportions. The Duchess of Bolton sat in the seat of honour, a monolithic pillar of disapproval. She ate almost nothing, but subjected each dish to a thorough and suspicious examination through a lorgnette she produced from somewhere in her purple draperies.

‘This soup,’ she remarked to the room at large, ‘has a curious flavour. Almost of… tomatoes.’

‘It’s our cook’s speciality, your Grace,’ said Mrs. Otis nervously. ‘Cream of tomato soup. It’s a very popular dish in the States.’

‘Indeed,’ said the Duchess. ‘How very… agricultural.’

She then turned her attention to Mr. Otis. ‘I understand, Minister, that you made your fortune in some kind of… product?’

‘That’s right, your Grace,’ said Mr. Otis, undeterred. ‘Otis’s Real Sensation Lubricator. A fine machine oil for all industrial and domestic purposes. We have a saying back home: If it squeaks, it needs an Otis.’

The Duchess’s lips tightened into a thin, bloodless line. ‘How fascinating. And your son,’ she said, turning her lorgnette upon Washington, ‘what is his chosen profession? Does he also lubricate?’

‘I am currently in a state of diplomatic contemplation,’ said Washington with a languid air he had been practising, ‘but I have a passion for gardening. I am trying to cultivate the American Beauty Rose here, but the English climate is proving stubbornly resistant to progress.’

‘Well, Virginia,’ he said, his voice retaining its usual business-like tone, though it was softened by a deep and abiding relief, ‘this is a most extraordinary turn of events. Mrs. Otis, who had been dabbing her eyes with a lace handkerchief, looked up in gentle protest. ‘Oh, Hiram, do not call it a transaction! It was an act of Christian charity, an errand of mercy. Our darling Virginia has saved a lost soul!’

‘Of course, my dear, of course,’ Mr. Otis agreed hastily. ‘An errand of mercy with, shall we say, a rather handsome honorarium. The point remains, what are we to do with this? ‘They are historical artifacts, not toys,’ Washington said sternly, his academic nature reasserting itself. ‘This parure has been the subject of at least three monographs. It was believed to have been lost in 1584, after Sir Simon’s unfortunate, ah, domestic incident.’

‘Well, it is found now,’ declared Mr. Otis, ‘and it belongs to Virginia. The ghost gave it to her, and possession, as they say, is nine-tenths of the law, even when the tenth part is supernatural.’

Throughout this discussion, Virginia herself had remained quiet, her gaze drifting from the glittering jewels to the face of the little Duke of Cheshire, who had not taken his adoring eyes off her since her return. He had recovered from his emotional display and was now perched on the arm of her chair, looking for all the world like a devoted knight-errant.

‘I do not want them, Papa,’ Virginia said softly, and the entire room fell silent once more.

‘Not want them?’ exclaimed Mrs. Otis. ‘But, darling, they are exquisite! That necklace would be perfect for your presentation at Court, once you are a Duchess!’

The little Duke blushed a brilliant crimson but looked even more smitten, if such a thing were possible.

‘Sir Simon gave them to me because he had nothing else to give,’ Virginia explained, her voice clear and simple. ‘They were part of his sorrow. He wanted me to have them as a token of his gratitude, but I do not think he would wish for us to quarrel over them. He is at peace now, and that is all the reward I could ever desire.’

Before Mr. Otis could formulate a reply to this display of what he considered beautiful but highly un-American sentimentality, the ponderous silence was shattered by a frantic ringing of the front doorbell. A collective groan went through the Otis family. Mr. Otis rose to his feet. ‘Lord Canterville? At this hour? What on earth can he want?’

‘I daresay,’ said Washington dryly, pushing his spectacles up his nose, ‘he has heard that the family ghost has been exorcised and the family jewels have been recovered. News travels rather fast when it has a fortune attached to it.’
